title: The risk of hypotension following co-prescription of macrolide antibiotics and calcium-channel blockers
authors: Wright AJ, Gomes T, Mamdani MM, Horn JR, Juurlink DN
population: Ontario residents aged 66 or older taking a single calcium channel blocker (verapamil, diltiazem, nifedipine, amlodipine or felodipine) and admitted to hospital for hypotension or shock; population-based nested case-crossover design comparing a 7-day risk interval with a 7-day control interval one month earlier
funder: This study was supported by the Institute for Clinical Evaluative Sciences (ICES), which is funded by an annual grant from the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care. The study was supported in part by the Ontario Drug Innovation Fund, which had no role in the design, analysis, conduct or reporting of the study.
authorConflicts: Mamdani has worked as a consultant for Pfizer, Novartis and Jansen-Ortho; Horn has consulted for Merck Consumer Care and writes books on drug interactions.
result: Of 7100 patients admitted with hypotension while taking a calcium channel blocker, 176 had a macrolide in the risk or control interval. Erythromycin, the strongest CYP3A4 inhibitor of the three, was associated with hypotension or shock (odds ratio 5.8, 95% CI 2.3 to 15.0), followed by clarithromycin (3.7, 2.3 to 6.1); azithromycin, which does not inhibit CYP3A4, was not (1.5, 0.8 to 2.8). Results were similar in patients taking only dihydropyridines (nifedipine, amlodipine or felodipine).
